strengths: WildFeedback addresses a relevant NLP problem: constructing preference data from naturally occurring user feedback. The pipeline is understandable, retains conversational context, and produces a substantial dataset of 20,281 expert-response pairs.

The GPT-4 data variant yields consistent improvements across three model families and three established benchmarks. Table 3 reports substantial length-controlled AlpacaEval 2 gains, including 24.3% to 34.9% for Phi 3 and 17.1% to 31.4% for Mistral. These results provide encouraging evidence of the training data’s usefulness.

The manuscript provides explicit rubrics, annotation and evaluation prompts, model versions, and major SFT/DPO hyperparameters. The human audit involving four annotators and 50 conversations provides useful validation of feedback detection. Holding out both users and conversations is an appropriate evaluation safeguard.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4o extracts preference summaries, generates expert positives, and judges responses using those summaries; on-policy pairs are also filtered for preference adherence. Checklist-based wins therefore leave correlated model biases unresolved. The human study validates SAT/DSAT detection, not summary faithfulness, preference-pair correctness, or trained model responses. Independent human assessment grounded in the original feedback is needed to establish the claimed improvement over conventional LLM judgment.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of natural user feedback. Models receiving SFT and DPO are compared only with their original instruction-tuned checkpoints. SFT-only and matched GPT-4 generation without feedback would help distinguish feedback-specific benefits from additional training and teacher distillation. There is also no matched training comparison with existing preference datasets. Comparing expert and on-policy variants additionally confounds response source with dataset size and filtering.

Population-level claims exceed the demonstrated coverage. Feedback occurs in only approximately 12.8% of source conversations, and DSAT detection has 48.4% recall and approximately 0.50 kappa against human labels. Although Section 4 explicitly targets common preferences, selecting central preferences within 70 clusters does not establish their prevalence among users. Evaluation on this curated, task-similar subset cannot substantiate the broader claims about diverse human values or overcoming selection bias. A randomly sampled held-out comparison and coverage analysis would clarify the supported scope.

The claim that either dataset variant preserves general performance contradicts Table 3. On-policy Mistral declines on AlpacaEval 2 LC from 17.1% to 12.9%, Arena-Hard from 12.6% to 10.3%, and MT-Bench from 6.71 to 6.42. These tradeoffs require explicit discussion. No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run results accompany claims of significant improvement, particularly limiting interpretation of the small gains in several on-policy settings.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendices. The dataset is only promised for future release, and the manuscript provides no code or split artifacts. The embedding model and precise clustering, selection, deduplication, and filtering procedures are insufficiently specified, as is the validation criterion used during hyperparameter search. The missing attribution controls and independent preference validation are decisive concerns for soundness; together with these reproducibility gaps, they warrant resubmission next cycle.
